segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Today's problem is a URL shortener that serves a billion redirects per month.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's pin down the read to write ratio first, because that single number drives most of the architecture.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Assume one hundred reads for every write. So roughly ten million new links a month and a billion redirects.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That is about four hundred redirects per second on average, and we should plan for peaks of maybe five times that during viral events.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The write path is small enough that a single primary database can handle it, but the read path needs aggressive caching.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Agreed. The functional requirements are simple. Create a short code for a long URL, redirect on lookup, and optionally expire the link.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should also support custom aliases, because marketing teams always want a readable code instead of a random string.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And analytics. Click counts, referrer, and rough geography are what customers actually pay for in this product category.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's start with code generation. How long should the short code be and what alphabet do we use?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Base sixty two, using digits and both letter cases. Seven characters gives about three point five trillion combinations, which is far beyond our needs.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Seven is a good default, but we could start at six and grow. Six characters is already fifty six billion possibilities.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The real question is how we pick a code. There are two families, random generation with a collision check, and deterministic encoding of a counter.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Counter encoding is attractive because it is collision free by construction. We take a globally unique integer and base sixty two encode it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But sequential integers leak information. Anyone can enumerate codes and walk the entire database of links, which is a privacy problem.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We can mitigate that by scrambling the counter with a reversible permutation before encoding, so the codes look random but remain unique.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: A Feistel network or simple multiplicative inverse modulo the key space works well for that. Unique, unguessable in practice, and no collision check needed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The alternative is random codes with an insert that fails on duplicate. At low fill ratios collisions are rare and a retry costs almost nothing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That is simpler to reason about and I would probably ship it first. The conditional insert makes correctness the database's job.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For the unique counter we could use a range allocator. Each application node grabs a block of a million identifiers and serves them locally.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That avoids a hot row and survives a brief outage of the allocator, since each node has a million identifiers buffered.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The cost is gaps in the sequence when a node restarts, but gaps do not matter at all for our use case.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's talk storage. The core table is the short code as primary key, the long URL, the owner, the creation time and the expiry.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: This is a pure key value access pattern, so a distributed key value store or a relational database with the code as the primary key both work.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I would pick a key value store partitioned by the short code, because our lookups never scan and never join on the hot path.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Ten million links per month is a hundred and twenty million a year, and each row is maybe five hundred bytes with the URL.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So around sixty gigabytes per year of primary data, which is small. The analytics events will be much larger than the link table.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For the read path, a cache in front of the store is essential. Link popularity follows a strong power law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: A small fraction of codes generate the overwhelming majority of redirects, so even a modest cache gets a very high hit ratio.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should cache the resolved long URL keyed by the short code, with a time to live and explicit invalidation when a link is edited or deleted.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Deleted links matter. If someone takes down a malicious link, a stale cache entry keeps serving it, so invalidation needs to be prompt.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We can publish invalidation events on a message bus and have every cache node subscribe, rather than relying purely on expiry.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For the redirect itself, do we return a permanent three oh one or a temporary three oh two?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Three oh two, because a permanent redirect is cached by the browser and we would never see the subsequent clicks.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Right, and we would lose analytics entirely for repeat visitors. The small extra load is worth keeping the data.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now the analytics pipeline. We should not write to the database synchronously on the redirect path.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Definitely not. We emit a click event to a queue, return the redirect immediately, and let a consumer aggregate asynchronously.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The consumer can roll the events into per link per hour counters, and we keep the raw events in cheap storage for a limited window.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should make the consumer idempotent, keyed on an event identifier, because at least once delivery means duplicates will happen.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's cover abuse, since URL shorteners are a favorite tool for phishing and malware distribution.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We need to scan submitted URLs against a reputation service at creation time, and rescan periodically because a clean domain can turn malicious later.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should also support an interstitial warning page for links flagged as suspicious, rather than a hard block in every case.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And rate limit link creation per account, because bulk creation of thousands of links is a strong abuse signal.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For availability, the redirect path must survive a regional failure. That argues for read replicas in multiple regions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Since links are immutable after creation in most cases, asynchronous replication is perfectly acceptable for reads.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The write path can stay in a single home region, and we accept slightly higher creation latency for distant users.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That asymmetry is the right call. Creation happens once, redirects happen a hundred times, so we optimize for the redirect.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: What about custom aliases colliding with generated codes? We need one namespace and a reservation mechanism.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I would reserve a separate prefix or length for custom aliases, so generated codes can never collide with user chosen ones.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Good. Let me summarize. Base sixty two codes from a scrambled counter, key value storage, heavy caching with event driven invalidation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Plus temporary redirects to preserve analytics, an asynchronous click pipeline, multi region read replicas and an abuse scanning layer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: I think the interesting part of this problem is how small the storage is and how much the design is really about cache and abuse.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Exactly. The naive version is a weekend project. The production version is mostly operational concerns around safety and read scale.
